source.excerpt: Twenty years from now you will be more disappointed by the things that you didn’t do than by the ones you did do. So throw off the bowlines. Sail away from the safe harbor. Catch the trade winds in your sails. Explore. Dream. Discover.
trail: Earliest known source, 1990: Quote Investigator finds no instance of the passage before H. Jackson Brown Jr.’s P.S. I Love You, where it sits among sayings credited to his mother.
Not in Twain: a Check Your Fact review rates the Twain attribution false, noting the lines appear nowhere in his collected works.
How the myth spread: Quote Investigator dates the earliest Twain-credited printing to a 1998 New Yorker advertisement, years after the 1990 book.

author.heading: About H. Jackson Brown Jr.
author.metaLine: 1940–2021 · American author, best known for Life's Little Instruction Book
author.bio: H. Jackson Brown Jr. was an American author from Tennessee who found enormous success with inspirational aphorism collections. His 1990 book P.S. I Love You gathered sayings he attributed to his mother, Sarah Frances Brown — and it is the earliest known home of this sailing passage. Brown’s later Life’s Little Instruction Book (1991) became a #1 bestseller.

misattribution.heading: How Twain got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s most reliably misattributed passages — a feel-good sailing metaphor pinned on Mark Twain, whose name is a magnet for uplifting lines he never wrote.

items.why: The lines are absent from Twain’s books, letters, and speeches. Quote Investigator finds no evidence connecting the passage to Twain and no appearance before 1990.

items.who: H. Jackson Brown Jr. (crediting his mother, Sarah Frances Brown)
items.why: The passage first appears in Brown’s 1990 collection P.S. I Love You, per Check Your Fact and Quote Investigator.

misattribution.truthLine: The safest statement: the wording is first documented in H. Jackson Brown Jr.’s P.S. I Love You (1990) — not anywhere in Mark Twain.

context.heading: Why the Twain label stuck
lead: Mark Twain is one of a handful of names — alongside Einstein, Gandhi, and Lincoln — that act as gravity wells for orphan quotations. A punchy, optimistic line with no obvious author drifts toward the most quotable famous person who plausibly could have said it, and Twain, the wry American adventurer, fits a sailing-and-exploration metaphor almost too well.

The irony is that Twain did write memorably about travel and risk — his 1869 The Innocents Abroad is a whole book about leaving the safe harbor. That thematic overlap makes the false attribution feel right, which is exactly why it spread so fast once it started.
context.pull: A famous name is easier to remember than a real one.
